title: Mappings and permutations
description: Questions on mappings, curves, one to one and onto, inverses, powers, permutations, cycles and signs.

questions.question: What makes a rule from a set $$S$$ to a set $$T$$ a mapping?
options: Every element of $$T$$ gets exactly one arrow in
Every element of $$S$$ gets exactly one arrow out
questions.explanation: A mapping gives each element of the domain exactly one value (:ref{#mapping}). Arrows arriving at $$T$$ can be any number, including none.

questions.question: Which rule is NOT a mapping from people to numbers?
options: Each person goes to the ages of their siblings
Each person goes to their height in cm
Each person goes to their birth year
Each person goes to the number $$7$$
questions.explanation: Someone with two siblings gets two values, and someone with none gets no value. A mapping needs exactly one (:ref{#mapping}).

questions.question: What is the image of the interval $$[-2, 1]$$ under $$x \mapsto x^2$$?
questions.explanation: Squares of numbers from $$-2$$ to $$1$$ run from $$0$$ (at $$0$$) up to $$4$$ (at $$-2$$) (:ref{#image-of-set}). The ends of an interval don't always go to the ends of its image.

questions.question: For $$f(x) = x^2$$ on all numbers, what is the preimage $$f^{-1}(\{16\})$$?
options: It doesn't exist, since $$f$$ has no inverse
questions.explanation: The preimage is every $$x$$ with $$x^2 = 16$$ (:ref{#preimage}). It makes sense for every mapping, with or without an inverse.

questions.question: Which of these can fail for a mapping $$f$$ and subsets $$A$$, $$B$$ of its domain?
questions.explanation: With $$f(x) = x^2$$, $$A = \{-3\}$$ and $$B = \{3\}$$: $$A \cap B$$ is empty, but $$f(A) \cap f(B) = \{9\}$$ (:ref{#mappings-unions}).

questions.question: Where is $$C(t) = (1 + 2t,\ 3 - t)$$ at $$t = 2$$?
questions.explanation: Put $$t = 2$$ into each coordinate (:ref{#parametrised-curve}): $$1 + 4 = 5$$ and $$3 - 2 = 1$$.

questions.question: $$(\cos t, \sin t)$$ and $$(\cos 2t, \sin 2t)$$, for all $$t$$, trace...
options: The same circle, at different speeds
questions.explanation: Both images are the unit circle (:ref{#trigonometry/unit-circle-point}); the second goes round twice as fast. A mapping knows when, its image only where (:ref{#parametrised-curve}).

questions.question: Which equation does $$C(t) = (t + 1,\ t^2)$$ trace?
questions.explanation: From $$x = t + 1$$, $$t = x - 1$$, so $$y = (x - 1)^2$$ (:ref{#curves-eliminate}). Check with $$t = 2$$: the point $$(3, 4)$$ fits.

questions.question: A ball is thrown level off a $$20$$ m cliff, with height $$20 - 4.9t^2$$ after $$t$$ seconds. When does it land?
questions.explanation: It lands when $$20 - 4.9t^2 = 0$$, so $$t = \sqrt{20/4.9} \approx 2.02$$. How fast it is thrown sideways doesn't change when it lands. Its path is a parabola (:ref{#curves-eliminate}).

questions.question: What does the polar map do to the vertical line $$r = 3$$?
options: Sends it onto the circle of radius $$3$$ about $$O$$
Sends it onto a line through $$O$$
Sends it onto a vertical line
questions.explanation: The pairs $$(3, \theta)$$ go to $$(3\cos\theta, 3\sin\theta)$$, all at distance $$3$$ from $$O$$ (:ref{#polar-map-images}).

questions.question: A mapping is one to one when...
options: At least one arrow arrives at each element
Exactly one arrow leaves each element
At most one arrow arrives at each element
questions.explanation: Two arrows arriving at one element means two inputs share a value (:ref{#injective}). At least one arriving is onto (:ref{#surjective}).

questions.question: Is $$x \mapsto x^2$$ from all numbers to all numbers one to one, onto, both or neither?
questions.explanation: $$3$$ and $$-3$$ share the value $$9$$, and $$-1$$ is never a value (:ref{#injective}, :ref{#surjective}). On the numbers $$\ge 0$$ it is both.

questions.question: $$x \mapsto 2^x$$ from all numbers to all numbers is...
options: Onto but not one to one
One to one but not onto
questions.explanation: Different inputs give different values (:ref{#functions/exponential-one-to-one}), but no value is $$0$$ or negative (:ref{#functions/exponential-positive}).

questions.question: Why must two of any $$13$$ people share a birth month?
options: A mapping from $$13$$ people to $$12$$ months can't be one to one
questions.explanation: That is the pigeonhole principle (:ref{#pigeonhole}): more elements than targets forces two arrows into one target.

questions.question: A mapping from a $$5$$-element set to itself is one to one. What follows?
questions.explanation: For mappings between finite sets of the same size, one to one and onto go together (:ref{#finite-injective-surjective}).

questions.question: Which mapping of the positive integers to themselves is one to one but not onto?
questions.explanation: Different $$n$$ give different $$2n$$, but odd numbers are never reached. For infinite sets one to one doesn't give onto (:ref{#finite-injective-surjective} needs finite sets). And $$n - 1$$ isn't a positive integer at $$n = 1$$.

questions.question: For $$f(x) = x + 2$$ and $$g(x) = 3x$$, what is $$(g \circ f)(1)$$?
questions.explanation: Do $$f$$ first: $$f(1) = 3$$, then $$g(3) = 9$$ (:ref{#mapping-composite}). Doing $$g$$ first would give $$5$$.

questions.question: When does a mapping have an inverse?
options: Exactly when it is one to one and onto
Exactly when it is one to one
questions.explanation: Turning every arrow round gives a mapping exactly when each element of the target has exactly one arrow in (:ref{#inverse-exists-bijective}).

questions.question: What is $$(g \circ f)^{-1}$$?
questions.explanation: Undo the last step first, like unwrapping a present before opening its box (:ref{#composite-inverse}).

questions.question: Can a mapping have two different inverses?
options: No: $$g = g \circ (f \circ h) = (g \circ f) \circ h = h$$
Yes, always two: left and right
questions.explanation: Grouping doesn't matter (:ref{#composite-laws}), and that chain shows any two inverses agree (:ref{#inverse-mapping-unique}).

questions.question: $$g \circ f = I$$ holds. Which must be true?
questions.explanation: If $$f(x) = f(x')$$ then $$x = g(f(x)) = g(f(x')) = x'$$. But $$f$$ need not be onto, so an inverse needs both equations (:ref{#inverse-mapping}).

questions.question: If $$h$$ has an inverse and $$h \circ f = h \circ g$$, what follows?
questions.explanation: Compose both sides on the left with $$h^{-1}$$ (:ref{#mapping-cancel}), just as you divide both sides of an equation by a non-zero number.

questions.question: For $$f(x) = x + 5$$, what is $$f^4(x)$$?
questions.explanation: Each step adds $$5$$, so four steps add $$20$$ (:ref{#mapping-powers}). The power counts repeats, not multiplication of values.

questions.question: What is $$f^0$$?
questions.explanation: Doing $$f$$ no times leaves everything where it is (:ref{#mapping-powers}).

questions.question: For a turn $$G$$ by $$\frac{\pi}{6}$$, what is $$G^{-3}$$?
questions.explanation: $$G^{-3} = (G^{-1})^3$$, three turns back by $$\frac{\pi}{6}$$ (:ref{#mapping-negative-powers}).

questions.question: If $$f^6 = I$$, what is $$f^{-1}$$?
questions.explanation: $$f \circ f^5 = f^6 = I$$, and the same on the other side (:ref{#repeating-inverse}).

questions.question: $$f$$ has an inverse, $$f^4 = I$$ and $$f^6 = I$$. What is the smallest power you can be sure is $$I$$?
questions.explanation: $$f^2 = f^6 \circ f^{-4} = I \circ I = I$$ (:ref{#powers-add-integers}). A turn by $$\pi$$ shows $$f$$ itself needn't be $$I$$.

questions.question: How is $$f^m \circ f^n = f^{m + n}$$ proved for all whole numbers?
questions.explanation: The case $$m = 0$$ is $$I \circ f^n = f^n$$, and each step uses $$f^{m + 1} = f \circ f^m$$ and grouping (:ref{#powers-add}).

questions.question: In two-row notation, the column with $$2$$ on top and $$5$$ below means...
questions.explanation: The bottom row says where each number goes (:ref{#permutation}).

questions.question: For $$\sigma = [1, 2]$$ and $$\tau = [2, 3]$$, is $$\sigma\tau = \tau\sigma$$?
options: No: one of them isn't a permutation
questions.explanation: $$\sigma\tau$$ does $$\tau$$ first: $$1 \to 1 \to 2$$, $$2 \to 3 \to 3$$, $$3 \to 2 \to 1$$. Composites of permutations are permutations, but order matters (:ref{#permutations-composite}).

questions.question: If $$\sigma(1) = 2$$, $$\sigma(2) = 4$$, $$\sigma(3) = 1$$, $$\sigma(4) = 3$$, what is $$\sigma^{-1}(1)$$?
questions.explanation: $$\sigma^{-1}(1)$$ is the number $$\sigma$$ sends to $$1$$ (:ref{#permutation-inverse}), which is $$3$$. The value $$\sigma(1) = 2$$ answers a different question.

questions.question: How many permutations of $$\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$$ are there?
questions.explanation: $$5! = 120$$ (:ref{#permutation-count}): five places for where $$5$$ goes, then $$4!$$ for the rest.

questions.question: About how many orders can a $$52$$-card deck be in?
questions.explanation: $$52!$$ has $$68$$ digits (:ref{#permutation-count}), so a well-shuffled deck is very likely in an order never seen before.

questions.question: What does the cycle $$[2, 5, 4]$$ say?
questions.explanation: Each number goes to the next, and the last goes back to the first (:ref{#orbit}).

questions.question: Which cycle is the same as $$[1, 4, 3, 2]$$?
questions.explanation: Starting from $$3$$: $$3 \to 2 \to 1 \to 4 \to 3$$. A cycle can start anywhere round its loop (:ref{#orbit}).

questions.question: Can two different orbits of a permutation share a number?
options: Yes, if they have the same length
No: two orbits are equal or have nothing in common
questions.explanation: If $$j$$ is in the orbit of $$i$$, following $$j$$ round traces the same loop (:ref{#orbits-disjoint}).

questions.question: A permutation has cycles of lengths $$2$$, $$3$$ and $$4$$. What is its order?
questions.explanation: Every cycle must come home together: the least common multiple of $$2$$, $$3$$ and $$4$$ is $$12$$ (:ref{#permutation-order}).

questions.question: $$i$$ lies in a cycle of length $$5$$. When is $$\sigma^t(i) = i$$?
questions.explanation: Divide $$t$$ by $$5$$: only the remainder matters (:ref{#cycles-orbit-powers}).

questions.question: How many perfect out-shuffles bring a $$52$$-card deck back to its starting order?
questions.explanation: Its cycles have lengths $$1$$, $$1$$, $$2$$ and six $$8$$s, whose least common multiple is $$8$$ (:ref{#permutation-order}).

questions.question: What is a cycle of length $$1$$?
options: A number the permutation doesn't move
questions.explanation: $$\sigma(i) = i$$ means $$i$$ is home after one step (:ref{#orbit}). These are usually left out of the decomposition (:ref{#cycle-decomposition}).

questions.topic: Swaps and the sign of a permutation
questions.question: How many swaps does it take to make a cycle of length $$6$$?
questions.explanation: A cycle of length $$k$$ is a chain of $$k - 1$$ swaps (:ref{#swaps-and-sign-cycle}).

questions.topic: Swaps and the sign of a permutation
questions.question: A permutation is a chain of $$7$$ swaps. Could it also be a chain of $$4$$?
options: No: the counts are both even or both odd
questions.explanation: Each swap changes the number of orbits by one (:ref{#swap-orbits}), which fixes the evenness of the count (:ref{#parity-theorem}).

questions.topic: Swaps and the sign of a permutation
questions.question: What is the sign of $$[1, 2, 3, 4]$$ as a permutation of $$\{1, \ldots, 5\}$$?
questions.explanation: It has $$2$$ orbits among $$5$$ numbers, so the sign is $$(-1)^{5 - 2} = -1$$ (:ref{#sign-from-cycles}). A $$4$$-cycle is $$3$$ swaps.

questions.topic: Swaps and the sign of a permutation
questions.question: Is a cycle of length $$3$$ even or odd?
questions.explanation: It is $$2$$ swaps (:ref{#swaps-and-sign-cycle}), so its sign is $$(-1)^2 = +1$$ (:ref{#permutation-sign}).

questions.topic: Swaps and the sign of a permutation
questions.question: $$\sigma$$ is odd and $$\tau$$ is odd. What is $$\sigma\tau$$?
questions.explanation: Signs multiply: $$(-1)(-1) = +1$$ (:ref{#sign-product}).

questions.topic: Swaps and the sign of a permutation
questions.question: How many of the $$24$$ permutations of $$\{1, 2, 3, 4\}$$ are even?
questions.explanation: For $$n \ge 2$$, exactly half are even (:ref{#half-even}): composing with $$[1, 2]$$ matches the even ones with the odd ones.

questions.topic: Swaps and the sign of a permutation
questions.question: Why can't the 15 puzzle swap just the 14 and 15 tiles?
options: The gap can never return home
Every slide sequence returning the gap home is an even permutation, and one swap is odd
questions.explanation: Each slide is a swap with the gap, and the gap changes square colour every slide, so returning home takes an even number (:ref{#swaps-and-sign-fifteen}).
